name: Page scaffold with Base layout, hero section, and section placeholders
steps: Navigate to http://localhost:4321/transformers/
Verify the page loads with the site header and footer (Base layout)
Verify a hero section with title 'How Transformers Work' (or similar) is visible
Verify placeholder sections exist for all major topics: Preamble, Architecture Overview, Embeddings, Attention, Multi-Head Attention, FFN, Residual Stream, Output, Circuits
Verify no build errors with pnpm build

name: Sticky table of contents with scroll-tracking
steps: Navigate to the transformers page
Verify a table of contents is visible in the sidebar (desktop) or collapsible (mobile)
Scroll through the page and verify the TOC highlights the current section
Click a TOC entry and verify smooth scroll to that section
Verify the TOC lists all major sections

name: Preamble section — motivation, historical context, and the promise
steps: Navigate to the transformers page
Verify the preamble section contains introductory text explaining what transformers are and why they matter
Verify a brief visual timeline or progression showing the evolution from RNNs/LSTMs to the attention mechanism
Verify the section ends with a 'teaser' — framing the transformer as a black box we're about to open

Verify the preamble establishes the VISUAL VOCABULARY that will be used throughout: introduce a consistent color scheme and shape language for the major components (e.g., a specific color for 'attention', another for 'FFN', another for 'embeddings') that all subsequent sections will reuse

name: Transformer architecture overview — interactive block diagram
steps: Navigate to the Architecture Overview section
Verify a diagram showing the full transformer architecture (embedding → N x [attention + FFN] → unembedding)
Verify the diagram uses the SAME color scheme and shape language established in the preamble's visual vocabulary
Verify the diagram is interactive: hovering or clicking a block highlights it and shows a brief tooltip/description
Verify an animation shows data flowing through the architecture end-to-end when triggered
Verify the diagram clearly labels: token embedding, positional encoding, attention blocks, FFN blocks, layer norm, residual connections, output layer
LINKAGE: This diagram is the 'map' for the rest of the page. Each subsequent section should feel like zooming into one block of this diagram. Verify that the section text frames it this way.

name: Tokenization explainer — text to tokens interactive
steps: Navigate to the Embeddings section

LINKAGE: Verify a visual transition or callout connects this section back to the 'token embedding' block in the architecture diagram from feature #4 — the reader should feel they are zooming into that first block
Verify an interactive widget where users can type text and see it split into tokens in real time
Verify tokens are color-coded and visually distinct (e.g., subword pieces shown differently)
Verify the token color-coding scheme introduced here is CONSISTENT and will be reused in all subsequent visualizations that show tokens
Verify explanatory text describes what tokenization is, why subword tokenization is used, and the vocabulary concept
Verify the widget handles edge cases gracefully (empty input, special characters)

name: Token embedding visualization — words as vectors in space
steps: Navigate to the Embeddings section (below tokenization)

LINKAGE: Verify this section begins by taking the tokens from feature #5 and showing the NEXT step — each token becoming a vector. The visual should show tokens (using the same color coding from #5) transforming into points in space
Verify a 2D or 3D scatter plot showing word embeddings in a reduced-dimensional space
Verify semantically similar words cluster together (e.g., 'king'/'queen', 'cat'/'dog')
Verify users can hover over points to see the word label
Verify explanatory text describes how tokens become high-dimensional vectors and why similar meanings produce nearby vectors
Verify the vector representation style (shape, color, size of vector arrows or dots) established here is CONSISTENT with how vectors will appear in subsequent attention and FFN sections

name: Positional encoding visualization — sine and cosine waves
steps: Navigate to the Positional Encoding subsection

LINKAGE: Verify a visual shows the embedding vectors from feature #6 being AUGMENTED with positional information — the reader should see the same vectors gaining an additional component, not a disconnected new diagram
Verify a visualization showing sine and cosine waves at different frequencies
Verify an interactive slider or scrubber lets users change the position index and see how the encoding vector changes
Verify a heatmap or stripe diagram shows the full positional encoding matrix for a sequence
Verify explanatory text covers: why position matters (attention is permutation-invariant), how sin/cos provide unique position signatures, and how the model uses these
LINKAGE: Verify the section ends by showing the combined embedding + position vectors as the INPUTS to the next section (attention). This is the handoff.

name: Single attention head — Q, K, V matrices explainer with animation
steps: Navigate to the Attention section

LINKAGE: Verify the section opens by receiving the combined embedding+position vectors from feature #7 — visually show THESE vectors (same style) entering the attention mechanism. Reference the architecture diagram: 'we are now inside the attention block'
Verify a visual showing an input sequence being multiplied by W_Q, W_K, and W_V matrices to produce Q, K, V
Verify the animation shows the matrix multiplication step by step — input vector goes in, Q/K/V vectors come out
Verify color coding consistently distinguishes Q (e.g., blue), K (e.g., orange), V (e.g., green) throughout — this Q/K/V color scheme must remain FIXED for all subsequent attention visualizations
Verify explanatory text uses the analogy: Q = 'what am I looking for?', K = 'what do I contain?', V = 'what do I offer?'
Verify the user can step through the animation or replay it

name: Single attention head — dot product attention and softmax interactive
steps: Navigate to the dot product / softmax subsection

LINKAGE: Verify the Q and K vectors shown here use the EXACT same color coding from feature #8 — the reader should recognize these as the same objects. Show Q and K vectors from #8 being brought together for the dot product
Verify a visualization showing Q·K^T dot products being computed between token pairs
Verify an interactive temperature slider shows how softmax sharpens or flattens the attention distribution
Verify the formula QK^T / sqrt(d_k) is shown and each component is explained
Verify a bar chart or similar shows the raw scores transforming into a probability distribution via softmax
Verify explanatory text covers: why dot product measures similarity, why we scale by sqrt(d_k), what softmax does

name: Single attention head — attention pattern heatmap
steps: Navigate to the attention heatmap subsection

LINKAGE: Verify the heatmap is presented as the RESULT of the Q·K dot products and softmax from feature #9 — not as an unrelated visualization. The transition should make clear: 'when we compute these scores for all token pairs, we get this matrix'
Verify a heatmap grid showing attention weights between all token pairs in an example sentence
Verify the example sentence is the SAME sentence used in features #8 and #9, so the reader can trace the same tokens through the pipeline
Verify hovering over a cell highlights the corresponding source and target tokens
Verify a color scale legend explains the attention weight values
Verify explanatory text connects the heatmap back to the Q·K computation from the previous section

name: Single attention head — value-weighted output animation
steps: Navigate to the value aggregation subsection

LINKAGE: Verify the V vectors shown here use the SAME color coding from feature #8, and the attention weights come from the heatmap in feature #10. The reader should see these two pieces — V vectors and attention weights — combining
Verify an animation showing attention weights being applied to V vectors and summed
Verify the visualization makes clear: high-attention tokens contribute more to the output
Verify the animation shows the weighted sum step: each V vector scaled by its attention weight, then all summed into the output vector
Verify a concrete example walks through one token's output computation from start to finish, using the SAME example sentence from features #8-10

LINKAGE: Verify a brief recap ties the full single-head pipeline together: input vectors → Q/K/V → dot product → softmax → weights × V → output. Show this as a mini-diagram that matches the visual language used throughout #8-11

name: Multi-head attention — why multiple heads and head specialization
steps: Navigate to the Multi-Head Attention section

LINKAGE: Verify this section opens by saying 'we just saw ONE attention head — now let's see what happens when we run SEVERAL in parallel'. Visually show the single-head diagram from #11's recap being duplicated into multiple parallel copies
Verify a visualization showing multiple attention heads operating in parallel on the same input
Verify 2-3 example heads are shown with different attention patterns (e.g., one for syntax/adjacency, one for coreference, one for positional)
Verify the heatmaps for each head use the SAME heatmap visual style from feature #10, so the reader recognizes them
Verify explanatory text covers: why one head isn't enough, how different heads learn different relationships, the analogy to looking at text from multiple perspectives

name: Multi-head attention — concatenation, projection, and interactive explorer
steps: Navigate to the multi-head concatenation subsection

LINKAGE: Verify a diagram shows the outputs from the parallel heads in feature #12 being concatenated into a single wide vector, then projected by W_O back to the model dimension. The head outputs should use the same visual style as #12
Verify an interactive explorer lets users toggle individual heads on/off and see how the combined output changes
Verify the visualization makes clear that each head operates on a subspace (d_model / n_heads dimensions)
Verify explanatory text covers the full multi-head formula: MultiHead(Q,K,V) = Concat(head_1,...,head_h)W_O
LINKAGE: Verify the section ends by showing the multi-head attention output as a vector in the SAME style as the input vectors, ready to be added back to the residual stream

name: Feed-forward network — structure, activation functions, and role
steps: Navigate to the FFN section

LINKAGE: Verify this section opens by receiving the output from multi-head attention (#13) through the residual connection. Show the same vector arriving at the FFN block — reference the architecture diagram: 'we are now in the FFN block, the second half of each transformer layer'
Verify a diagram showing the two-layer FFN structure: linear → activation → linear
Verify an interactive activation function plot lets users compare ReLU, GELU, and SiLU with a toggle
Verify the expansion ratio (d_model → 4*d_model → d_model) is visualized as a 'bulge' or expansion/compression
Verify explanatory text covers: what the FFN does after attention (per-token processing), the 'memory' or 'lookup' interpretation, why the expansion matters
LINKAGE: Verify the section ends by showing the FFN output being added to the residual stream, completing one full transformer layer

name: Residual connections and layer normalization
steps: Navigate to the Residual Stream section

LINKAGE: Verify this section ties together the data flow from features #8-14, showing the residual stream as the 'highway' that attention (#8-13) and FFN (#14) contribute to. Use the same vector visual style throughout
Verify a visualization showing the residual stream as a 'highway' with attention and FFN as on/off ramps
Verify an animation demonstrates: input + attention_output = residual, then residual + ffn_output = next_residual
Verify layer normalization is shown as a 'normalization gate' that stabilizes values
Verify an interactive widget shows how layer norm transforms a set of values (before/after)
Verify explanatory text covers: why residual connections enable deep networks (gradient flow), why layer norm helps training stability
LINKAGE: Verify the section shows how stacking N of these layers (attention + FFN + residual) creates depth, connecting back to the architecture diagram from #4

name: Output layer — unembedding, logits, and next-token prediction
steps: Navigate to the Output section

LINKAGE: Verify this section receives the final residual stream vector from #15 and shows it entering the unembedding layer. Frame this as 'the vector has traveled through all N layers and is now ready to become a prediction'. Connect visually to the 'unembedding' block in the architecture diagram from #4
Verify a visualization showing the final hidden state being projected to vocabulary-sized logits via the unembedding matrix
LINKAGE: Verify the unembedding is explicitly framed as the REVERSE of the embedding from feature #6 — reuse the same visual language to show the symmetry
Verify a bar chart shows the top-k predicted tokens with their probabilities
Verify an interactive temperature slider lets users adjust sampling temperature and see probabilities redistribute
Verify explanatory text covers: unembedding as the reverse of embedding, softmax over vocabulary, temperature's effect on creativity vs. determinism

name: Full architecture animated walkthrough — bringing it all together
steps: Navigate to a 'Putting It All Together' section (or return to the architecture diagram)

LINKAGE: This is the CULMINATION. Verify it reuses the architecture diagram from feature #4 but now enhanced — each block can be expanded or highlighted to show the detailed visualization from its corresponding section (#5-16)
Verify a full end-to-end animation traces a token through every layer: embedding → positional encoding → attention → residual → FFN → residual → ... → unembedding → prediction
Verify the animation reuses the EXACT visual language from earlier sections: same token colors (#5), same vector styles (#6), same Q/K/V colors (#8), same heatmap style (#10), same FFN bulge (#14)
Verify play/pause/step controls allow the user to control the animation pace
Verify each step briefly highlights or annotates what computation is happening
Verify this section feels like a satisfying culmination — the black box from the preamble (#3) is now fully opened

name: Circuits — composing attention heads into functional units
steps: Navigate to the Circuits section

LINKAGE: Verify this section builds on multi-head attention (#12-13) by showing that heads across DIFFERENT layers can compose. Reuse the head heatmap style from #12 but now show information flowing between layers
Verify explanatory text introduces the concept of circuits: attention heads composing across layers to implement algorithms
Verify a concrete example of an induction head circuit is visualized (head in layer N copies patterns that head in layer N-1 identified)
Verify the visualization shows information flow across layers between specific heads
Verify the connection to mechanistic interpretability is made: we can reverse-engineer what these circuits compute

name: Mechanistic interpretability teaser and future post link
steps: Navigate to the final section
Verify a brief teaser describes what mechanistic interpretability is and why it matters (safety, understanding)
Verify a mention of the planned follow-up post (reproducing mechinterp locally with Llama 3)

LINKAGE: Verify the section ends by tying back to the preamble (#3) — we promised to open the black box, and now we have. The closing should reference the journey: tokens → embeddings → attention → FFN → prediction → circuits
Verify there is a clear visual ending to the page (not just text trailing off)

name: Scroll-triggered animations and section transitions
steps: Scroll through the entire page from top to bottom
Verify visualizations animate in as they enter the viewport (not all loaded at once)
LINKAGE: Verify section transitions reinforce continuity — each section's entry animation should feel like a continuation of the previous section's conclusion, not a disconnected appearance
Verify no janky layout shifts as elements animate in
Verify animations use IntersectionObserver or similar for performance (no scroll event listeners)
Verify animations respect prefers-reduced-motion media query

name: Mobile responsive layout for all sections and visualizations
steps: View the page at 375px width (iPhone SE) and 768px width (iPad)
Verify the TOC collapses to a hamburger or top bar on mobile
Verify all interactive visualizations are usable via touch (no hover-only interactions)
Verify text is readable without horizontal scrolling
Verify visualizations resize or reflow appropriately (not just clipped)
Verify no horizontal overflow on any viewport size

name: Performance audit — lazy loading, animation efficiency, bundle size
steps: Load the page and verify initial load does not block on off-screen visualizations
Scroll through the entire page and verify smooth 60fps scrolling (no jank)
Verify heavy visualizations (3D, canvas) are lazy-initialized when they enter the viewport
Verify the page builds successfully with pnpm build and no TypeScript errors
Verify no console errors or warnings in the browser dev tools
